Logroño flood adaptation: future rainfall raises building-level flood risk; planned nature-based solutions offset little; untargeted greening favours the less vulnerable

An independent replication — 5 limbs, composed into one finding.

AF Anne Fouilloux ORCID 0000-0002-1784-2920 · published 2026-10-11
  • Topics

What is being replicated

Three FORRT chains from one shared analysis of building-level pluvial flood risk in Logroño (Spain), under REACHOUT's flood scenarios, give one picture.

The bottom line
Uses conclusions from · Validated Uses conclusions from · Validated Uses conclusions from · Validated Cites as data source · Partially Supported Tested · Validated

Recommendation: Adaptation planning in Logroño should assume that the pluvial flood risk of today's 100-year design storm will be reached by the 50-year storm under the median EURO-CORDEX scenario and by the 25-year storm under the 90th percentile (2041-2070), and should test measures under both scenarios; the Destination Earth Climate DT supports the median scenario's order of magnitude.

Three FORRT chains from one shared analysis of building-level pluvial flood risk in Logroño (Spain), under REACHOUT's flood scenarios, give one picture. (1) Heavier future design rainfall puts more residents in buildings at pluvial flood risk in every case examined (all return periods from 2 to 200 years, both EURO-CORDEX future scenarios, each risk index): +1.5 to +5.9 % under the median scenario and +5.0 to +9.5 % under the 90th percentile; today's 100-year storm becomes a 50- or 25-year storm. The Destination Earth Climate DT supports the median scenario's order of magnitude and places the 90th percentile at the high end. (2) REACHOUT's planned nature-based solutions offset only a small part of this: they reduce the number of residents at risk by less than 4 %, only for frequent storms, and not at all during the 100- and 200-year storms. (3) Converting all open space to green surfaces takes about 9 to 21 % of the residents at risk out of risk, but mainly the less socially vulnerable ones: in all 40 comparisons the residents taken out of risk are less vulnerable than those who remain, and the most vulnerable fifth benefits least. Together: climate change raises flood risk for Logroño's residents, the measures planned so far do little against it in this model, and greening placed without regard to vulnerability mainly protects those who need it least.

The replication limbs

Replication 1 of 5

City-wide greening takes mainly less socially vulnerable residents out of pluvial flood risk in Logroño

ValidatedModerateUses conclusions from

Validated. In Logroño (Spain), converting all open space to green surfaces takes about 9 to 21 % of the residents at pluvial flood risk out of risk, and these are mainly the less socially vulnerable residents.

Full conclusion

Validated. In Logroño (Spain), converting all open space to green surfaces takes about 9 to 21 % of the residents at pluvial flood risk out of risk, and these are mainly the less socially vulnerable residents. In every one of 40 comparisons (3 climates, 7 return periods, 2 risk indices, one map missing) the residents taken out of risk are less vulnerable on average than those who remain at risk, significantly so in 26 and never the other way. The most vulnerable fifth of residents benefits least: of its residents at risk, typically under 2 % leave risk for the 25-year storm and rarer ones, against 12 to 30 % of the least vulnerable fifth. The pattern is not a clean gradient across all five groups: the fourth fifth benefits strongly for some rare storms. The finding matters for adaptation planning: greening placed without regard to vulnerability mainly protects those who need it least, which argues for targeting measures to where vulnerable residents are at risk.

Replication 2 of 5

REACHOUT's planned nature-based solutions reduce residents at pluvial flood risk in Logroño by less than 4 %

ValidatedModerateUses conclusions from

Validated. In Logroño (Spain), the nature-based solutions of REACHOUT's planned scenario reduce the number of residents in buildings at pluvial flood risk only a little and only for frequent storms: by at most 1.7 % without the extra ponds and 3.7 % with them, and not at all during the 100- and 200-year storms, under present or future rainfall.

Full conclusion

Validated. In Logroño (Spain), the nature-based solutions of REACHOUT's planned scenario reduce the number of residents in buildings at pluvial flood risk only a little and only for frequent storms: by at most 1.7 % without the extra ponds and 3.7 % with them, and not at all during the 100- and 200-year storms, under present or future rainfall. The planned scenario without ponds stops reducing risk after the 10-year storm, the version with ponds after the 50-year storm. Neither ever increases the number of residents at risk. The measures change the flood maps over a few hectares in the south of the city, while future rainfall adds tens to over a hundred hectares of deeper water (see the future-rainfall chain), so in this model the planned measures do not offset climate change. This describes the measures as REACHOUT modelled them, as infiltration and storage in a fill-and-spill model without sewers; it is not an assessment of the measures as they may be built.

Full replication chain →Jupyter BookRepositoryArchived release
Replication 3 of 5

Future design rainfall increases residents in buildings at pluvial flood risk in Logroño

ValidatedModerateUses conclusions from

Validated. In Logroño (Spain), with the current green cover, the heavier future design rainfall of the REACHOUT scenarios puts more residents in buildings at pluvial flood risk than present-day rainfall in every case examined: all seven return periods (2 to 200 years), both future scenarios (EURO-CORDEX median and 90th percentile) and each risk index of the framework.

Full conclusion

Validated. In Logroño (Spain), with the current green cover, the heavier future design rainfall of the REACHOUT scenarios puts more residents in buildings at pluvial flood risk than present-day rainfall in every case examined: all seven return periods (2 to 200 years), both future scenarios (EURO-CORDEX median and 90th percentile) and each risk index of the framework. No building moves to a lower risk class. In effect, today's 100-year storm becomes a 50-year storm under the median scenario and a 25-year storm under the 90th-percentile scenario. How large the increase is depends on how much heavier the rainfall becomes: REACHOUT's median scenario is of the same order as the Destination Earth Climate DT estimates for La Rioja, while its 90th-percentile scenario lies above all of them, so the larger increases are a high-end case.

Replication 4 of 5

Building-level pluvial flood risk mapping more accurate than sub-city units

Partially SupportedModerateCites as data source

Partially supported. The paper states that building-level granularity "has the potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of urban risk assessments".

Full conclusion

Partially supported. The paper states that building-level granularity "has the potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of urban risk assessments". Transferred to Logroño (Spain) with open data only, the framework's hazard component is accurate where it can be checked: places where recorded storms (2018-2024) caused flooding are among the most flooded places in the open 2 m flood map (REACHOUT), far more than other streets, for every design storm. The finer granularity is what makes the difference: the same flood map summarised per census section (the sub-city statistical units the paper moves away from) locates the same places clearly less well. This supports the claim, including its comparison with sub-city units, for the part of a risk assessment that says where water causes problems.

The claim as a whole, about risk assessments, could only be partly tested. Risk = social vulnerability x exposure x hazard, and recorded impacts (press reports of flooded streets, underpasses, garages, a hospital car park) say where water caused trouble, not who was affected or how vulnerable they were. Social vulnerability was therefore not tested, and exposure only indirectly. The building-level risk indices agree only weakly with the recorded places; this is expected by design (several reported places are roads and underpasses with no residents beside them, where the framework correctly gives high hazard but low risk to residents) and is not evidence against them. The accuracy of the building-level risk classes themselves remains unvalidated.

Replication 5 of 5

Building-level pluvial flood risk of Vogelbacher et al. (2026) reproduced with an independent open implementation

ValidatedHigh Confidence

Validated. On the authors' own example, an independent open implementation reproduces the paper's building-level pluvial flood risk and its pattern: every building falls in the same risk class as in the authors' ArcGIS results, for both risk to well-being and risk to mobility and accessibility, and the highest risks are where high exposure and high hazard coincide, as the paper states.

Full conclusion

Validated. On the authors' own example, an independent open implementation reproduces the paper's building-level pluvial flood risk and its pattern: every building falls in the same risk class as in the authors' ArcGIS results, for both risk to well-being and risk to mobility and accessibility, and the highest risks are where high exposure and high hazard coincide, as the paper states. Reproducing the numbers required following the authors' results and scripts where they differ from the paper's text (sensitivity weights, TOPSIS normalisation, and rings that exclude neighbouring buildings). An existing open implementation run as is does not reproduce them, mainly because it recomputes exposure and keeps neighbouring footprints in the hazard rings.

Full replication chain →Jupyter BookRepositoryArchived release

Recommendations

  1. Adaptation planning in Logroño should assume that the pluvial flood risk of today's 100-year design storm will be reached by the 50-year storm under the median EURO-CORDEX scenario and by the 25-year storm under the 90th percentile (2041-2070), and should test measures under both scenarios; the Destination Earth Climate DT supports the median scenario's order of magnitude.
  2. Nature-based solutions should be placed according to where socially vulnerable residents are at risk, not according to available open space: converting all open space to green surfaces mainly takes less vulnerable residents out of risk.
  3. The small effect of REACHOUT's planned nature-based solutions (less than 4 % fewer residents at risk, none for the 100- and 200-year storms) should be re-assessed with a hydrodynamic model that represents storage, overflow and the sewer network, and with the measures' actual layout, before it is used to accept or reject them; in SaferRAIN they enter only as infiltration and terrain changes.
  4. The layout of planned measures and the scenario inputs should be published openly, so that their effect can be reproduced and compared across models.

Where this holds

Logroño municipality (La Rioja, Spain), every residential building inside the area modelled by all REACHOUT scenarios (4,540 buildings with residents). Hazard: REACHOUT SaferRAIN pluvial flood maps (2 m, 15-minute design storms, return periods of 2 to 200 years) for the current green cover, REACHOUT's planned scenario with and without extra ponds, and all open space green; present rainfall from station data and future rainfall scaled by EURO-CORDEX changes (2041-2070, median and 90th percentile), checked against the Destination Earth Climate DT (IFS-NEMO SSP3-7.0 projections to 2049 and storylines of 2017-2024 at +2 °C). Risk: the Vogelbacher et al. (2026) framework (social vulnerability x exposure x hazard) through building-climate-risk v0.2.1, residents from the 2021 census, vulnerability from census-section indicators; classes with present-day limits. All three chains use the same analysis release (10.5281/zenodo.23298913).

Limitations

The three findings come from one analysis and one flood model; they are consistent with each other by construction and are not independent confirmations. SaferRAIN is a fill-and-spill model without sewers on 15-minute design storms; it represents nature-based solutions only as infiltration and terrain changes, which likely understates storage and drainage effects. The future rainfall is a scaling of observed design storms; REACHOUT's factors cannot be reproduced exactly from its EURO-CORDEX file and the Climate DT check is single-model and hourly. Social vulnerability comes from census-section rates and was not validated against impact data; residents are fixed at 2021; 1,851 residents near the edge of the modelled area are left out. The all-green scenario is a bound, not a plan, and REACHOUT's planned scenario may differ from what the city builds. Results are scenarios for one city and may not transfer to cities with other terrain, drainage or social geography.

Plain-language summary

Will heavy rain flood more homes in Logroño, and do green spaces help?

iRecommended reading level — General public — no science background needed

This study looked at every residential building in Logroño and asked how many residents are at risk when a short, heavy downpour floods the streets — today, with heavier future rain, and with more green space in the city.

What was looked at

The study used computer flood maps of Logroño made by the REACHOUT project for 15-minute downpours, from storms expected every 2 years to storms expected once in 200 years. For each residential building it combined three things: how deep the water gets nearby, how many people live there, and how socially vulnerable they are. It compared today's rain with heavier future rain, the green measures planned in REACHOUT's scenario, and an extreme case where all open space becomes green.

Heavier rain puts more people at risk

With heavier future rain, more residents live in buildings at risk in every case examined: a few percent more in the middle scenario, and up to about one in ten more in the high one. How much more depends strongly on how much heavier the rain becomes, which is itself uncertain. Put simply, the flooding we expect today from a once-in-100-years storm could come roughly twice as often, or more in the high scenario. Data from the European Destination Earth project support the middle scenario's order of magnitude.

The planned green measures help only a little

The planned measures, as REACHOUT modelled them, reduce the number of residents at risk by a few percent at most, only for frequent storms, and not at all for the biggest storms (once in 100 or 200 years). In this model, they do not offset the effect of heavier rain.

More green space helps — but not the people who need it most

Turning all open space green takes roughly one in ten to one in five of the residents at risk out of risk. But these are mainly less socially vulnerable residents: in every comparison made, the residents who leave risk are less socially vulnerable than those who stay at risk, and the most vulnerable fifth of residents benefits least.

What it means, and what it cannot say

The study recommends placing green measures where vulnerable residents are at risk, not simply where there is open space, and checking the planned measures again with a model that includes sewers and storage, using their real layout. These are scenarios from one flood model, not predictions, and the uncertainties are large: the model has no sewers, the future rain is a scenario, vulnerability is estimated from census areas, and the measures may work differently when built. The direction of each finding is more reliable than its exact size.

Heavier rain is expected, though by how much is uncertain; where green measures are placed decides who they protect.

Plain-language summary

Who is protected when a city goes green?

iRecommended reading level — Secondary school · ages ~13–16

Climate change makes heavy rain heavier. Cities can add green spaces, which let rain soak into the ground. This study asks a fair question: who does that protect?

The question

Logroño is a city in northern Spain. When a lot of rain falls in a short time, streets and underpasses can flood. This is called pluvial flooding: flooding caused directly by rain, not by a river. The study asks three things. Does heavier future rain put more people at risk? Do the planned green measures help? And when the city goes green, who is protected?

The test

Scientists used flood maps made by a computer model. For every home building, they combined three things: how deep the water gets nearby, how many people live there, and how vulnerable they are — for example, young children or older people living alone. A '100-year storm' means a storm so strong that, on average, it comes once in 100 years. They tested storms from every 2 years to every 200 years.

The result

Heavier future rain puts more people at risk in every case tested. The planned green measures cut the number of people at risk only a little, and not at all for the biggest storms. Turning all open space green helps more: roughly one in ten to one in five of the people at risk become safe. But most of them are the less vulnerable people. The most vulnerable fifth of residents benefits least.

The lesson: how science checks itself

Before using the method, it was checked. First, the method was rebuilt independently with open tools: every building got the same risk class as in the original study. Second, the flood maps were compared with places that really flooded in Logroño: they matched well, but this only partly confirmed the whole method, because real flood reports do not say who was affected. Finally, every result here comes from one computer model, with large uncertainties: for example, the model has no sewers, and nobody knows exactly how much heavier future rain will be. So scientists trust the direction of a result (more risk, small help, unequal help) more than its exact number, and they say so.

Being fair is part of the science: a good plan asks not only how much it helps, but whom.
